milestones.note: Deterministic rules make no API calls and cost nothing, so an analysis without LLM rules completes with zero LLM calls and zero cost.

milestones.note: `truecourse analyze --no-llm` skips the LLM rules for that run.

milestones.note: `truecourse analyze` stores its results as plain JSON files under `.truecourse/` in the analyzed repository.

milestones.note: `.truecourse/LATEST.json` holds the most recent analysis snapshot.

milestones.note: After an analysis, `truecourse list` prints the violations that analysis found.

milestones.claimTitle: analyze catches code-quality problems
milestones.note: Analysis reports Code quality violations such as magic numbers, empty catch blocks, console.log calls, cognitive complexity, unused variables, redundant code, and missing type hints.

milestones.claimTitle: analyze catches security problems
milestones.note: Analysis reports Security violations such as SQL injection, hardcoded secrets, eval usage, insecure random, XSS, path traversal, and unsafe deserialization.

milestones.claimTitle: analyze catches bugs
milestones.note: Analysis reports Bugs-category violations such as race conditions, type mismatches, mutable defaults, implicit optional, off-by-one, and unchecked returns.

milestones.claimTitle: analyze catches architecture problems
milestones.note: Analysis reports Architecture-category violations such as circular dependencies, layer violations, god modules, dead modules, tight coupling, and cross-service imports.

milestones.claimTitle: analyze catches performance problems
milestones.note: Analysis reports Performance violations such as N+1 queries, O(n^2) string concatenation, unnecessary allocations, missing pagination, and sync I/O in async code.

milestones.claimTitle: analyze catches reliability problems
milestones.note: Analysis reports Reliability violations such as unhandled promises, resource leaks, missing timeouts, swallowed exceptions, and unsafe error handling.

milestones.claimTitle: analyze catches database problems
milestones.note: Analysis reports Database violations such as missing indexes, missing transactions, lazy loading in loops, raw SQL bypassing the ORM, and schema issues.

milestones.claimTitle: LLM rules require a configured LLM transport
milestones.note: LLM rules require a configured LLM transport, so requesting them without one does not produce LLM results.

flows.notes: The category claims are proved by SEEDING the doc's own named example and asserting the violation the rule reports, not by binding a real codebase: `truecourse list` prints `<icon> <SEVERITY>  <title>` and carries neither the rule key nor the category, so "a Database-category violation" is only observable as the titled finding ("SELECT * in production code"). A real codebase would make the assertion structural (count > 0) and would prove nothing about the category. The flow also opens with the two paths a first-time user hits before anything works — `truecourse analyze` with no LLM decision in a non-interactive shell (exit 1) and `--llm` with no transport configured — the second of which is the claim `llm-rules-require-an-llm-transport`.

the `~/.truecourse/registry.json` entry (analyze registers the repo)
seedable: a small polyglot project, one file per rule category, each file carrying ONE canonical example the docs name (console.log, eval, a mutable Python default, an import cycle, a regex built inside a loop, a bare JSON.parse, a `SELECT *` query)
a git repository with a single commit holding those files, so the tree is clean and no stash decision is reachable on this path
env — `TRUECOURSE_HOME` pointed inside the sandbox (never the developer's home) and `TRUECOURSE_TELEMETRY=0`

milestones.note: The hook reads its policy only from `<repo>/.truecourse/hooks.yaml`, so editing that file changes the hook's behavior.

milestones.claimTitle: block-on accepts the five documented severities
milestones.note: `block-on` accepts the severities info, low, medium, high, and critical.

milestones.claimTitle: a deleted hooks.yaml makes the hook warn
milestones.note: If `hooks.yaml` is deleted, the hook warns on the commit.

milestones.claimTitle: a deleted hooks.yaml passes every commit
milestones.note: If `hooks.yaml` is deleted, the hook passes every commit rather than applying hidden code-level defaults.

flows.notes: The conflicting-state corner: the same commit is blocked under one policy and allowed under another, and then allowed again with NO policy at all. Honest scope on `block-on-accepts-five-severities` — the scenario proves all five values are ACCEPTED (`hooks status` renders the policy and exits 0) and that a non-default severity genuinely changes the verdict (a low violation blocks once `low` is listed); it does not manufacture one violation per severity, which no seed can guarantee.

stepCreatable: the baseline, the hook, and the seeded policy file (analyze, git, hooks install)
seedable: the rewritten `hooks.yaml` bodies: a narrowed `block-on: [critical]`, then the full five-severity list
a git repository, identity, and the violation-bearing files each policy is tested against
env — `TRUECOURSE_HOME`, `TRUECOURSE_TELEMETRY=0`, `TRUECOURSE_LLM_TRANSPORT=claude-code`

flows.title: A team turns on LLM rules for the pre-commit hook
flows.goal: A team turns on LLM rules for the pre-commit hook

milestones.claimTitle: setting llm true runs LLM rules on every commit
milestones.note: Setting `pre-commit.llm` to `true` in hooks.yaml makes the hook run LLM rules on every commit, spending tokens per commit.

flows.notes: The second configuration path of the hook policy. JOURNEY GAP recorded while authoring: `hooks run`'s promised stdout is one progressive line and a verdict — it carries no LLM usage or cost line — so "spending tokens per commit" is not directly observable on the public surface. The scenario proves the policy is HONORED instead of merely stored, with two observations the journeys do promise: `hooks status` reports "LLM rules on commit: enabled (tokens per commit)", and the same commit under the same policy with the transport made unusable fails with the LLM-configuration exit 1 rather than passing deterministically. The residue (usage on stdout) is a journey defect worth fixing, not a reason to weaken the assertion.

stepCreatable: the baseline, the hook and the policy file
seedable: a `hooks.yaml` with `pre-commit.llm: true`
a git repository, identity, and a change to commit
env — `TRUECOURSE_HOME`, `TRUECOURSE_TELEMETRY=0`
supplied: claude-code-cli — the `claude` binary, logged in. Unregistered ⇒ this variant blocks alone while the default `llm: false` hook flow keeps running.

flows.title: A repository with a file the scanner cannot finish still produces a report
flows.goal: A repository with a file the scanner cannot finish still produces a report

milestones.claimTitle: TRUECOURSE_DET_FILE_TIMEOUT_MS overrides the per-file budget
milestones.note: Setting `TRUECOURSE_DET_FILE_TIMEOUT_MS` (in milliseconds) overrides the deterministic scan's per-file time budget.

milestones.claimTitle: a file over the per-file time budget is skipped with a warning
milestones.note: A single file that exceeds the deterministic scan's per-file time budget is skipped with a warning instead of freezing the run.

milestones.claimTitle: the analysis always completes and writes its output
milestones.note: Even when files are skipped for exceeding the per-file time budget, the analysis completes and writes its output.

flows.notes: The budget is driven from the documented env override rather than by authoring genuinely pathological source (catastrophic backtracking is not a thing a scenario can seed deterministically). The control step — the same project at the default budget, no skip warning — is what makes the override claim falsifiable rather than a tautology.

stepCreatable: the store and the analysis output that must exist even when a file was skipped
seedable: one large but entirely legitimate generated-looking source file (a few thousand lines), plus one ordinary file whose violation must still be reported
env — `TRUECOURSE_DET_FILE_TIMEOUT_MS` set to a value small enough that the large file cannot finish; the same run without it is the control

milestones.claimTitle: analyzing C# without the Roslyn host fails fast
milestones.note: Analyzing a repository that contains C# without the Roslyn host built fails fast rather than falling back to a partial analysis.

flows.notes: Stands alone deliberately: a `.cs` file makes analysis fail hard by design, so folding it into any other flow would poison that flow's analyze steps. flows.goal: A developer keeps generated, vendored and ignored files out of the analysis

milestones.claimTitle: analyze honors .gitignore
milestones.note: Analysis honors the repository's `.gitignore`, so files git ignores are not analyzed.

milestones.claimTitle: nested .gitignore files are honored
milestones.note: Analysis honors nested `.gitignore` files, not just the one at the repository root.

milestones.claimTitle: .git/info/exclude is honored
milestones.note: Analysis honors `.git/info/exclude`.

milestones.claimTitle: the configured global excludes file is honored
milestones.note: Analysis honors the user's configured global git excludes file.

milestones.claimTitle: .truecourseignore excludes tracked paths from analysis
milestones.note: A `.truecourseignore` at the repository root excludes the paths it matches from analysis even though git still tracks them.

milestones.claimTitle: .truecourseignore uses .gitignore syntax
milestones.note: `.truecourseignore` uses the same syntax as `.gitignore`, supporting `#` comment lines, directory patterns such as `src/generated/`, and specific file paths such as `scripts/ingest-epub.js`.

milestones.claimTitle: patterns are anchored to the file's location
milestones.note: Patterns are anchored to the location of the `.truecourseignore` file, so `src/generated/` matches only the top-level `src/generated` directory.

milestones.claimTitle: **/ patterns match at any depth
milestones.note: A pattern such as `**/generated/` excludes matching directories at any depth.

flows.notes: The anchoring claim and the globstar claim CONTRADICT each other in one file (`src/generated/` must leave `lib/src/generated/` analyzed, which `**/generated/` then excludes), so the scenario runs them as two stages of the same file with an analysis between them. `core.excludesFile` is set repo-locally inside the sandbox; the developer's real global git config is never touched, which is a hard requirement of this flow, not a detail.

stepCreatable: the store and each analysis snapshot
seedable: violation-bearing files at every exclusion source: root `.gitignore`, a nested `.gitignore`, `.git/info/exclude`, a repo-local `core.excludesFile`, and paths matched by `.truecourseignore`
one control file that is never excluded — without it, an empty report would 'prove' every exclusion claim at once
`.truecourseignore` bodies written in two stages: first with the three documented forms (comment, `src/generated/`, `scripts/ingest-epub.js`), then with `**/generated/` added
a git repository and identity
env — `TRUECOURSE_HOME`, `TRUECOURSE_TELEMETRY=0`

noFlowClaims.claimTitle: ships 1,500+ deterministic rules and 100 LLM rules
noFlowClaims.reason: unobservable via CLI (pending review). The claim asserts a SPLIT (deterministic vs LLM) and `truecourse rules list`'s promised output — `Rules for <repo>: N shown (E enabled, D disabled)` plus per-rule rows of key / status / [domain/severity] / language support / name — carries no deterministic-vs-LLM label. Asserting only the total (>1,600 rows) would be a green that does not prove its claim, exactly the defect class the fidelity judge exists to catch. Two ways out, both for the user to choose: label the kind in `rules list` output, or narrow the doc claim.

noFlowClaims.claimTitle: the per-file budget defaults to 30 seconds
noFlowClaims.reason: unobservable via CLI (pending review). Nothing prints the effective budget, so the only proof is a wall-clock measurement: a file that must survive 29s and be skipped at 31s. That is a minutes-long, machine-speed dependent scenario — the flakiness it buys is worse than the coverage. The override claim (`TRUECOURSE_DET_FILE_TIMEOUT_MS`) IS carried, in `survive-a-file-that-exceeds-the-per-file-budget`.

noFlowClaims.claimTitle: C# is supported with the .NET 8 SDK
noFlowClaims.reason: needs dotnet-sdk. A supplied dependency with no registered instance: the .NET 8 SDK plus the Roslyn host built from the TrueCourse source tree. Register one and this becomes a flow (seed a `.cs` file, assert a violation against it) — the scenario is blocked, not impossible.

noFlowClaims.claimTitle: C# semantic rules need the Roslyn host built once
noFlowClaims.reason: needs dotnet-sdk, and the documented build command (`dotnet build -c Release tools/csharp-roslyn-host`) points INSIDE the TrueCourse source tree, which a user who installed from npm does not have. Blocked on both the supplied SDK and a doc/journey answer to "where does an installed user build the host from".

noFlowClaims.claimTitle: disabling a rule removes its detection and LLM cost
noFlowClaims.reason: llm-cost plus an unassertable comparison. The falsifiable half is "the run's LLM call/token totals DROP after the rule is disabled", which needs two full LLM runs over the same project and a comparison BETWEEN their summaries; a scenario asserts per-step matchers, not deltas across steps, and the model's own output is not deterministic enough to assert the rule's absence directly.

noFlowClaims.claimTitle: .truecourseignore also narrows spec scan doc discovery
noFlowClaims.reason: out of the authored journey set — the proof runs through `truecourse spec scan` and `.truecourse/specs/corpus.json`, and no `cli/spec` journey exists in reference/journeys (the reference covers the code-analysis surface: analyze, add, list, rules, hooks, root). It also needs an LLM transport for a full scan. The claim belongs to a spec-scan area flow once that surface's journeys are authored.
